\section{Complexifying demand-only shocks}\label{sec:beyond-demand-only}

\subsection{Kaldor--Verdoorn dynamics}\label{subsec:pricing-capacity}
% Provenance: ADR-0029, ADR-0031, ADR-0032; runs pricing_capacity-v2-GAMMA-*,
% pricing_mobile-v2-ALPHA-* and pricing_capacity_rows-v1-{BF,ALPHA,BETA,DELTA}-*
% (OpenCGE v0.2.1, value-added-scaled exponent; supersede the v1 capacity
% runs); Table~\ref{tab:pricing-kaldor} is generated by
% revision/tables/make_pricing_door.py. Numbers below are cited by run id.
A key observation from the preceding section is that the one-factor model shows a limited price response, and one that appears only where the labour market is sector-specific: the deflator moves in the no-reallocation and elastic-supply columns and stays at one in the other nine cells of Table~\ref{tab:results-matrix}. The nature and scope of a transformational stimulus --- especially in a long-term setting --- nevertheless invite reflection on how a permanent shift in demand could affect production in the short and medium run: will additional demand enable firms to exploit greater economies of scale? can it spur research and investment, so that production becomes more effective over time? or will it induce capacity pressure, thereby reducing efficiency? Such concerns -- which can be reformulated as the question of where we sit on the standard cost curve -- would indeed impact prices and they can be captured on a different level, namely that of technology.

The most straightforward way to express this intuition formally is to let
effective technology respond to utilisation,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-door}
  A^{\mathrm{eff}}_i \;=\; A_i\,\Bigl(\frac{y_i}{\lambda_i}\Bigr)^{-\delta_i\,\alpha_i},
\end{equation}
with $\lambda_i$ as the sector's baseline gross output and $\alpha_i$ the factor (value-added) share, so that $\delta = 0$ reproduces the model of the preceding sections exactly.
The elasticity $\delta_i$ is a reduced-form utilisation elasticity of \emph{value-added} productivity, not a rental rate: no factor is added and no income block is created, because the productivity change passes into unit cost under zero profit, weighted by the factor share. A Hicks-neutral gain $d\ln A^{\mathrm{eff}}_i$ then raises value added per worker by $d\ln A^{\mathrm{eff}}_i/\alpha_i$ (Appendix~\ref{app:pricing-hooks}), so $-\delta_i$ is directly comparable with an estimated Verdoorn coefficient.\footnote{Applied to gross output without the factor share, the same bracket would overstate the value-added response by $1/\alpha_i$: factor shares below one half turn $\delta = 0.5$ into an elasticity above one, and into $11.6$ for coke and refined petroleum ($v \approx 0.04$).}

The two signs of $\delta$ again carry two traditions, underpinned by two distinct visions of the typical operating mode of an economy. With $\delta > 0$ scarcity gains an additional bite: unit costs rise with own output --- capacity pressure, tight supply chains, higher risk and, hence, eventually higher costs and prices (even if, as here, market power considerations are bracketed out). With $\delta < 0$, on the other hand, unit cost falls with output --- the dynamic increasing returns articulated early by \textcite{Verdoorn1949} (see also \citealp{Kaldor1966} and \citealp{SylosLabini1995}).\footnote{With $\delta_i < 0$ a sector's unit cost falls as its output rises --- a positive feedback that can admit several equilibria. Every run with $\delta \neq 0$ is therefore reachedby continuation in $\delta$ from the $\delta = 0$ case and re-solved from four starting points; a result is accepted only if the converged starts agree to $10^{-6}$ and the residual Jacobian has full rank. Every result with $\delta \neq 0$ in the executed generation passes this check(Appendix~\ref{app:pricing-guard} reports the design and the measured spreads).}

We run scenarios with $\delta = \pm 0.5$ for manufacturing to illustrate the impact of the Verdoorn coefficients on estimated outcomes. These effects are confined to the
goods sectors (CPA sections A--F: agriculture, mining, manufacturing, utilities
and construction), following \textcite{Kaldor1966}, who reads Verdoorn's law
as a law of manufacturing, not of services. Moreover, this setup matches the incidence of the programme, whose direct demand falls entirely on goods sectors. The counterfactual that extends the elasticity to the services sectors as well is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:variants}.\footnote{Extending the elasticity to the services sectors also leaves the sign of the price response unchanged in the four closures where quantities absorb the shock --- the deflator still rises with $\delta > 0$ and falls with $\delta < 0$. However, the sign reverses where the real wage is pinned: at $\delta = -0.5$ the deflator then rises by 0.14 and 0.03 percent under preference reallocation and tax finance and falls only under external finance ($-0.82$ percent). The main reason for this is that service sectors  lose demand in this scenario, which translates into lower productivity -- and that loss is passed straight into prices.}

Table~\ref{tab:pricing-kaldor} reports the results for such scenarios by building on the outcomes already shown in Section~\ref{sec:application} to cover the full matrix of approaches discussed for scenarios with endogenously increasing ($\delta = -0.5$) and decreasing ($\delta = +0.5$) productivity effects. For these values we observe small changes in the aggregate price level across all scenarios relative to the baseline applications. Deviations from baseline values thereby follow a similar pattern: all outcomes show the same sign as well as similar magnitudes imposing net changes of the price level ranging from $0.05\%$ to about $0.4\%$ with the large majority of estimates lying below $0.2\%$. While all models now show some response in prices, the no-reallocation and the elastic labour supply model -- which also came with price responses already in Table~\ref{tab:results-matrix} --- still show the most pronounced change in prices on both, aggregate as well as sectoral levels (the latter is partially captured by $\max |\Delta p|$)

These price changes reflect efficiency gains and losses due to the additional demand that have different implications for production and employment across different model specifications. For labour market closures where scarcity governs economic reactions -- that is, the first three closure specifications in our matrix -- increasing technological capabilities ease these scarcity constraints so that production can expand. For the output adjustment closures with a pinned real wage on the other hand,  increasing efficiency leads to lower employment effects and, correspondingly, (slightly) lower impacts on net welfare because the size of output adjustment is determined ex ante (and can now be achieved with fewer inputs).

Notably, we observe that the different financial closures have close to no impact on how the economy responds to introduction of Kaldor--Verdoorn effects for the models based on constrained factor supply, whereas it has, as in the preceding section, a stronger influence on the outcome of the quantity adjustment model based on fixed wages. A similar discrepancy is observed for the positive Kaldor--Verdoorn term. In the no-reallocation, standard-CGE and elastic-supply closures, tax finance and external finance continue to produce identical real outcomes when productivity responds to output. Moreover, we observe that the perfect correspondence between the fixed-wage and Leontief columns observed for the baseline case breaks for any $\delta \neq 0$: in such a case, where prices move, substitution elasticities matter again and the coincidence dissolves. In general, the fixed wage model thereby shows greater responsiveness in output to technological change as compared to the Leontief closure: Under external finance a negative Kaldor--Verdoorn term implies an increase of employment by $1.35\%$ against the $1.48\%$ shown for the Leontief closure.

\subsection{Markup-Pricing and distributional assumptions}\label{subsec:pricing-markup}
% Provenance: ADR-0029 (Stage A), ADR-0030 (Stage B), ADR-0032; runs
% pricing_markup-v2-* and pricing_profit-v2-* (all five labour rows,
% OpenCGE v0.2.1; supersede the v1 markup runs); Table~\ref{tab:pricing-markup}.
While Kaldor-Verdoorn dyamics capture the idea that firms become successively more efficient when supplying greater quantities, such an increase in firm size can also lead to a corresponding increase in market power. Similarly, effective markups are said to rise with utilisation, which  points to the relevance of distributional considerations in input-output models with multiple production factors. All this eventually resonates with the observation that pricing power that moves with demand has a long pedigree in economics \citep{Kalecki1954,Bils1987}. Taking the latter formualtion -- markups rising with capacity utilization -- and projecting it unto a sectoral level in line the basic setup from section \ref{sec:kernel}, we arrive the the following formulation for prices 

\begin{equation}\label{eq:markup-door}
  p_i \;=\; \mu_i\,c_i, \qquad \mu_i \;=\; 1 + \kappa\Bigl(\frac{y_i}{\lambda_i} - 1\Bigr),
\end{equation}
which is nested at $\kappa = 0$. Introducing such a pricing equation gives profits an explicit role which is why this section departs from the hitherto used benchmark case of a one factor model, but introduces capital as a second factor of production. This feature ???

%NOTE: wir haben hier wieder mal ein lamlbda eingeführt?
% Ist das OG lambda


This section uses it only as a pricing
closure, not as a theory of distribution. Two modelling choices make
it a closure. First, firms still hire labour and inputs at \emph{marginal
cost} $c_i = p_i/\mu_i$, while households and other firms buy at $p_i$; the
four places where the price enters a first-order condition are re-derived
accordingly in Appendix~\ref{app:pricing-door}. Second, the rent
$\Xi = \sum_i (1 - 1/\mu_i)\,p_i y_i$ must go somewhere.

Table~\ref{tab:routing} lists the four places it can go. Foreign owners would
book it in the external account; a government wedge would make the state a
third financing instrument beside F2 and F3. We take \emph{retention} as the
baseline (the retained rows of Table~\ref{tab:pricing-markup}): the rent is booked as
saving by firms, the household budget is unchanged and all real effects run
through relative prices. Retention is the cheapest closure that keeps the
external-account identity exact; its cost, stated rather than implied, is that
retained funds are hoarded, since investment is exogenous. We develop the
domestic-profit alternative (the distributed rows): the household receives
$(1 - s_\pi)\Xi$ untaxed and saves the rest at the retention rate $s_\pi$,
with $s_\pi = 1$ reproducing retention exactly.

\toprule

\midrule

\caption{Where the markup rent can go: the assumption-disclosure table for

\input{tables/table7_pricing-markup.tex}

Run against the capacity door, the markup door turns a robustness check into a
result. At the fixed real wage, with the capacity door confined to the goods sectors,
every door raises the price level in every financing column except
Kaldor--Verdoorn, which lowers it in all three (the fixed-wage panels of
Tables~\ref{tab:pricing-kaldor} and~\ref{tab:pricing-markup}).
Both doors move sectoral prices by the same order of magnitude. At
$\kappa = 0.5$ the markup's largest sectoral deviation (9 to 12 percent) is
two to two and a half times the capacity door's. The doors part company in the quantity block,
where the rent shows up as a leak (retention) or as additional household
demand (distribution). Whether a demand-led transformation raises or lowers
prices therefore depends on which pricing door is modelled, on which sectors
it acts and on how the programme is financed. Under external finance the
bracket runs from a 0.35 percent fall (Kaldor--Verdoorn in goods;
\texttt{pricing\_capacity-v2-GAMMA-F3-dm05-s0}) to a 1.83 percent rise
(distributed markup; \texttt{pricing\_profit-v2-GAMMA-F3-k05-spis}). Capacity
pressure (0.34 percent) and the retained markup (1.01 percent) lie in between;
the all-sector profile widens the fall to 0.82 percent
(Appendix~\ref{app:variants}). The profit share stays small --- below two
percent of factor income in every cell --- and rises with the financing
closure's demand impulse. Distributing the rent raises consumption and
employment relative to retention in every financing column of the fixed-wage
and Leontief panels, most under external finance. In the three CPI-gauge
panels of Table~\ref{tab:pricing-markup} it changes nothing: the distributed
rows repeat the retained rows exactly, because the net external transfer $F$
falls by precisely the
distributed rent (\texttt{pricing\_markup-v2-ALPHA-F2-k05} against
\texttt{pricing\_profit-v2-ALPHA-F2-k05-\{spi05,spis\}}), the same mechanism
that makes tax and external finance indistinguishable there, so the routing of
the rent matters only where the real wage is pegged. The welfare measure
changes meaning accordingly: with distributed
profit, $\Delta W$ is the consumption of a household that also owns the
firms, and each manifest carries a real-income companion (labour plus
distributed profit, deflated by the CPI) beside it. Two caveats bound the
reading: the markup is symmetric about the baseline, so a contracting sector
prices at a discount ($\mu_i < 1$; the run records the range), and leaving the
rent untaxed understates the fiscal response under tax finance.

% Against this backdrop we concede that the introduction of Leontief-like properties in the production function helps bridging paradigmatic cleavages on a level of conceptual foundations -- e.g. with respect to the question how to adequately represent production processes. However, we find that introducing such a conceptual shift in neoclassical IO-models will actually serve to increase the gap between both approaches in terms of predicted outcomes. This result is not too surprising when taking into account that the assumption of a Leontief technology implies less flexibility as compared to a Cobb-Douglas technology. Hence, in the context of assumptions on substitutability neoclassical approaches are more optimistic than the heterodox archetype: viewed in isolation greater substitutability comes with higher prospects for growth in case of demand shocks and, correspondingly, leads to a more positive assessment of fiscal intervention in terms of forced green investment. However, this relatively more optimistic stance does in no way compensate for the fact that the estimated growth effects remain negative, which is effectively driven by assumptions on capacity constraints. However, before turning to this key aspect in section \ref{sec:labor} further below, we first inspect structural differences between model outcomes on a more granular level.

The key requirement is the willingness to assume that such an expansion of the labor force is indeed a plausible reaction -- either due to labor market considerations or as a general response to increased effective demand. While this feature is not truly surprising it shows how modifying dominant convictions on the role and modeling of capacity constraints indeed opens up a shared realm, in which the simplistic juxtaposition of an 'expansionary' Leontief-approach and a 'contractionary' CGE-perspective becomes subject to a more nuanced perspective that allows for pragmatically interpreting labor slack as a moderating variable to explore some shared ground between these two competing visions of the economy.
